It had just launched the first iPhone when the recession began in a market still dominated by BlackBerry.

   But Apple’s return was eclipsed by auto parts retailer O’Reilly Automotive, up close to 5,000%. AutoZone, which releases results tomorrow, was close behind.

   It sounds impossible: Americans don’t buy more cars today than they did in 2007, and each one still has the same number of wiper blades and taillights. EVs don’t even need motor oil.

   The performance of those retailers was driven by smart financial stewardship and the resilience of their business models. But their Apple-like gains were measured a year ago. Rising interest rates and gasoline prices are enough to foul even the finest engine. 

   AutoZone is down 31% over the past year and is likely to echo the downbeat message from competitors O’Reilly and Advance Auto Parts when it reports. That suggests a hopeful pattern. 

   Just like during the 2008-2009 recession, when oil prices hit their all-time high, deferred maintenance from the retailers’ financially pinched lower-income clientele hurts sales at first. By the fall of 2008, the three stocks were down by 30% on average while Walmart shares were up for the year.

   Food is a necessity. Eventually, though, spark plugs are too. 

   And, instead of being tied to new auto sales, that actually has an inverse correlation with maintenance. AutoZone had great years for same-store sales in 2009, 2011, 2020 and 2021 when car sales were lousy and the vehicle fleet got older. The sweet spot for parts sales is cars between 4 and 11 years old.

   Sinking money into your jalopy has a higher payoff when a new or lightly used car is out of reach financially—maybe not at first, but increasingly so as old cars face wear and tear. That pain point hinges somewhat on weather, with snowy winters boosting customer traffic.

   Sales and sentiment turned several months into the 2008-2009 recession. Back then, depressed share prices gave these serial buyers of their own stock extra bang for the buck. AutoZone has bought back three-quarters of its shares since the end of the 2007 fiscal year. O’Reilly has repurchased more than half of its shares over a similar span.

   From the recession’s start through the end of 2011, AutoZone and O’Reilly shares beat the S&P 500 by 161% and 128%, respectively. Economic conditions then were certainly worse than today—unemployment is half as high as in 2011. The stocks aren’t as cheap either.

   O’Reilly and AutoZone’s recent slumps leave them at modest premiums to their respective trailing 10-year averages of price to forward sales.

   Investors aren’t being offered quite the same bargains as in 2008, but it’s time to start kicking the tires.

Greased Lightnin’

 

If investors were asked a year ago to guess the most successful consumer stock since the global financial crisis, many would have said Apple. It had just launched the first iPhone when the recession began in a market still dominated by BlackBerry.

 

But Apple’s return was eclipsed by auto parts retailer O’Reilly Automotive, up close to 5,000%. AutoZone, which releases results tomorrow, was close behind.

 

It sounds impossible: Americans don’t buy more cars today than they did in 2007, and each one still has the same number of wiper blades and taillights. EVs don’t even need motor oil.

 

The performance of those retailers was driven by smart financial stewardship and the resilience of their business models. But their Apple-like gains were measured a year ago. Rising interest rates and gasoline prices are enough to foul even the finest engine. 

 

AutoZone is down 31% over the past year and is likely to echo the downbeat message from competitors O’Reilly and Advance Auto Parts when it reports. That suggests a hopeful pattern. 

 

Just like during the 2008-2009 recession, when oil prices hit their all-time high, deferred maintenance from the retailers’ financially pinched lower-income clientele hurts sales at first. By the fall of 2008, the three stocks were down by 30% on average while Walmart shares were up for the year.

 

Food is a necessity. Eventually, though, spark plugs are too. 

 

And, instead of being tied to new auto sales, that actually has an inverse correlation with maintenance. AutoZone had great years for same-store sales in 2009, 2011, 2020 and 2021 when car sales were lousy and the vehicle fleet got older. The sweet spot for parts sales is cars between 4 and 11 years old.

 

Sinking money into your jalopy has a higher payoff when a new or lightly used car is out of reach financially—maybe not at first, but increasingly so as old cars face wear and tear. That pain point hinges somewhat on weather, with snowy winters boosting customer traffic.

 

Sales and sentiment turned several months into the 2008-2009 recession. Back then, depressed share prices gave these serial buyers of their own stock extra bang for the buck. AutoZone has bought back three-quarters of its shares since the end of the 2007 fiscal year. O’Reilly has repurchased more than half of its shares over a similar span.

 

From the recession’s start through the end of 2011, AutoZone and O’Reilly shares beat the S&P 500 by 161% and 128%, respectively. Economic conditions then were certainly worse than today—unemployment is half as high as in 2011. The stocks aren’t as cheap either.

 

O’Reilly and AutoZone’s recent slumps leave them at modest premiums to their respective trailing 10-year averages of price to forward sales.

 

Investors aren’t being offered quite the same bargains as in 2008, but it’s time to start kicking the tires.
